Part A — Creating Data Frames
```{r}
# TODO: Create three vectors of equal length (5 students):
# name (character): "Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"
# age (numeric): 20, 21, 19, 22, 20
# passed (logical): TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")

age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)

passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
name
age
passed
```
Answer: The vector "name" stores the students name, "age" stores their age and "passed" stores whether they passed or failed. 
```{r}
# TODO: Combine name, age, and passed into a data frame called students
# using data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
# Print students

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students
```
Answer: Same with the previous one, but this time I used data.frame to combine the three vectors into one table, where each row represents a student and each column contains their informatio (age and passed/failed). It also looks much organized and only prints "students" unlike the last one where i have to print it each vector.
```{r}
# TODO: Check the type of the "name" column using typeof(students$name)
# and class(students$name)

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```
Answer: Both result shows "character" since the values stored in those are text values. 
```{r}
# TODO: Now create a SECOND data frame called courses directly, without
# separate vectors first, using data.frame() with these columns:
# course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103")
# units = c(3, 3, 2)
# instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")

courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)

courses
```
Answer: I use data.frame to combine the course, unit, and instructors in one table. This one is much shorter compared to the first data.frame. It didnt create a seperate vector, but rather create it inside the data.frame and the output still the same but shorter code. 


Question #1

You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline.
Both approaches produce the same kind of object.
In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

Answer: The data.frame requires same length to match it with information, otherwise it will show an error, no output unlike with the previous exercise. 

Question #2

A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”
Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

Answer: A data frame is like a list because each column can have a different data type since they are separate vectors. However, each column should contain one data type to keep the values consistent. Example: Name("Characters only), Age("Numeric only), and Passed(True/false only). If it was mix in one column like mix("char", "num", " TRUE") and by using class funtion, it would show "character".

Part B — Subsetting Data Frames
```{r}
# TODO: Access the "age" column of students three different ways:
# students$age
# students[["age"]]
# students["age"]  -- note: compare the output/class of this one to the others

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students$age
students[["age"]]
students["age"]
```
Answer:The first two methods return the age column as a vector, while students["age"] returns it as a data frame with one column.
```{r}
# TODO: Access the entire 2nd row of students using students[2, ]

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students[2, ]
```
Answer: It shows ben, his age and if he passed or failed because students[2, ] accesses the second row and all columns.
```{r}
# TODO: Access the value in row 3, column "name" using students[3, "name"]

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students[3, "name"]
```
Answer: The Output is "Cid" since students[3, "name"] accesses the 3rd row and "name" column. 
```{r}
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE
# Hint: students[students$passed == TRUE, ]

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```
Answer:the output showed only Ana, Ben, and Dex because they are the students who passed.
```{r}
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE AND
# age is greater than 19. Use the & operator to combine both conditions.

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
```
Answer: the output still shows the 3 students who passed but this time their age is included. 


Question #3

students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.
Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

class(students$age)
class(students["age"])
```
Answer: students$age returns a numeric vector, while students["age"] returns a data frame. Like lists, single brackets keep the structure, while double brackets extract the element.

Question #4

In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows.
What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

Answer: if i use the | (Or) instead of &(And) operator, it would show more result since the | operator needs only one true condition, while & operator needs both conditions to met.

Question #5

Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name).
Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

Answer: age shows the max, min and mean, for passed, it counts the TRUE/FALSE values, while name shows the length and type of text. A mean wouldnt make sense on "name" since its a text, not numbers.

Answer: str() would be useful for checking the structure of data frame while summary() if i want to see the summaries and statistics of its column. 

Part D — Data Frame Operations
```{r}
# TODO: Add a new column called year_level to students with values:
# 2, 3, 1, 4, 2  (one per student, in the same order as the rows)

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)

students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
students
```
Answer: I added a new column called year_level containing the students year levels.
```{r}
# TODO: Remove the "passed" column from students by setting it to NULL
# students$passed <- NULL

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)

students$passed <- NULL
students
```
Answer: I figured it out that it has other ways to removed vector, first option was by removing it or removing the passed column from the data frame using NULL. 
```{r}
# TODO: Sort students by age in ascending order using order()
# Hint: students[order(students$age), ]

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)

students[order(students$age),]
```
Answer: by using the order, students age are sorted from youngest to oldest (ascending order). 
```{r}
# TODO: Sort students by age in DESCENDING order
# Hint: use order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), or order(-students$age)

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)

students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
Answer: By using order again but this time with dreasing = TRUE, students age are arranged from the oldest to youngest (Dreasing order).


Question #7

After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?
Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)

students <- data.frame(name, age, passed)

students$passed <- NULL

students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```
Answer: No, it will not work since we removed that column by assigning it to null so R return an empty output. It is important to keep on track with my data.frame because some operation remove or add columns. Knowing the structure would help me avoid those errors.


Question #8

order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.
Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

Answer: order() arranges the ages in ascending order by default, so it returns 3, 1, 5, 2, 4. These numbers are the row index numbers. When used with "students[order(students$age), ]", those positions are used to rearrange the entire rows, including all columns.

Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge
```{r}
# TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of
# midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)
grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
grades
```
Answer: the output shows the students name, their midterm and final term grades and lastly the newly added column average, solve their average by adding the midterm and final term then dividing it by 2 to get the result for each student. 
```{r}
# TODO: Print only the rows of grades where remarks is "Failed",
# showing just the name and average columns.
# Hint: grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]

grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
```
Answer: This time i added the remark column to identified who failed by mentioning their name and average only. The result shows only Eli with an average of 72.5 and didnt meet the condition that i assumed was 75.


Question #9

Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”
Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

Answer: I would create a column to calculate the difference between the midterm and final scores of every student. Then, I would arrange the results in descending order to identify who has the highest score difference. Another step is to add a column using the condition "midterm >= 75" to check whether the midterm score might have a big impact on their average grade.

Conclusion
In 3–4 sentences, summarize what a data frame is, how it relates to vectors and lists from earlier labs, and why it is R’s primary structure for real-world tabular data.

Answer: A data frame is a table that contains rows and columns. It is like a list because each column is a separate vector that can have a different data type. It is useful in R because it organizes data into an understandable table.
